title_en: Chinese Humor (16/20): Fifty Famous Mix-ups from Sound-Alike Words
note_en: Not one story but a whole collection: fifty famous cases where an accent, a dialect or just words that sound alike in Chinese led to confusion, jokes or superstition, from the classic "porridge" heard as "face-washing water" and the tongue twister about "four" and "ten," to number plates full of eights, unlucky names and look-alike characters that trip up even foreign students.

sentences.en: China officially has more than seven dialect regions, while Mandarin has only a few hundred usable syllables, which have to cover tens of thousands of Chinese characters.

sentences.en: Someone hears 稀饭 "porridge" as 洗脸水 "face-washing water"; a southern customer orders rice noodles in a northern restaurant and is served a bowl of wheat noodles; and an old joke says someone heard "it's raining" (下雨) as "it's raining fish" (下鱼); at a hospital registration window someone heard 大夫 "doctor" as 大户 "rich family"; and someone else heard 睡觉 "sleep" as 水饺 "dumplings," and became a laughing stock.

sentences.en: When someone is asked what they'd like to eat and casually says 随便 "whatever," the other person really does serve them "whatever": a bowl of plain rice; the phrase 我想死你了 "I miss you to death" often gives Chinese beginners a fright; when booking a hotel, the words 方便 "convenient" and 房间 "room" are easy to mix up when said quickly; 老师 "teacher" and 老实 "honest" differ only in tone, yet people keep mishearing them; and the tongue twister "four is four, ten is ten" often makes people talk faster and faster until they end up arguing.

sentences.en: Crosstalk comedians often deliberately "mishear" a simple greeting as a completely different sentence to get a laugh; whole crosstalk routines are sometimes built entirely on two performers mishearing each other's homophones; and the answers to many character riddles are actually hidden by homophones; at New Year people give apples, because the 苹 in 苹果 sounds like the 平 in 平安 "safe and sound," making them a gift wishing for safety; while giving a clock (送钟) sounds like 送终 "attending someone's deathbed," so in many places it's an absolute no.

sentences.en: The three characters 己, 已 and 巳 look almost the same but mean completely different things, and students often can't tell them apart; 大, 太 and 犬 differ by just one dot yet mean completely different things, a classic trap for beginners; and teachers often put 甲, 由, 申 and 田 together as a little memory game for students; 乌 and 鸟 differ by a single stroke but are two completely different characters, and even many foreign students get them wrong; 人 and 入 look like mirror images, and beginners often write them the wrong way round by accident.
